definition: Inure means to make someone accustomed to something unpleasant.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word inure. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know inure should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Two seasons of subway commutes had inured Malik to shoulder-to-shoulder crowds.
To familiarize just makes something known — it stops short of inure, which toughens you against something genuinely unpleasant.
Numb goes further than inure: the inured worker still feels the hardship and bears it, while the numbed one has stopped feeling it at all.

To harden is to toughen generally -- against weather, pain, or criticism -- and it needs no history: one brutal season can harden you. Inure works only by repeated exposure, the slow grind of the same hardship met again and again. Hardening is the armor; inuring is the wear that built it.

To toughen is to build resistance, physical or mental, and it is often deliberate -- coaches toughen recruits on purpose. Inure is what long exposure does on its own: the hardship stays unpleasant, but becomes bearable. You toughen for what is coming; you are inured to what you have already borne.

To accustom is simply to make familiar through repetition, and it accepts anything -- pleasant, neutral, or grim. Inure is the narrow case: only unpleasant things qualify, borne until bearable. You become accustomed to Saturday pancakes; you are inured to the five a.m. train platform in January.
to shelter from every discomfort
to make more responsive to it, not less

Inure hides no prefix and no Latin root: it is the old phrase 'in ure' — in use, in practice — welded into one word. Ure itself, a medieval noun for work or use, has vanished from English entirely, so there is no cousin left to compare.
Inure means to make someone accustomed to something unpleasant.
Guides on the high tea route are inured to the thin air that leaves their clients gasping at every switchback; four years of carrying loads up the pass will do it.
Inure is habituation to something unpleasant, and it keeps its preposition: inured to the cold, to criticism, to noise.
Being inured is not numbness — the hardship is still felt, just bearable — and pleasant routines don't qualify: nobody is inured to Saturday pancakes.
Inure is the formal verb for exposure doing its slow work, always to something unpleasant: hardship, noise, criticism.
Accustom covers pleasant and neutral routines; numb means the feeling itself has died.
If the thing is nice, you have simply gotten used to it.

Arroyo ate lunch in her car because the cafeteria felt like standing inside a bell.
There was no trick to what happened next, and no program: just lunch duty, five days a week, year after year.
By her eighth autumn the roar was unchanged and she was not.
Colleagues marveled that years of that din had inured her to it.
She corrected them on one point: it still gave her a headache most Fridays.
It had simply stopped deciding where she ate.
The new hires who fled to their cars each noon regarded her, over their steering wheels, with something like awe.
